title: Jamal Wallace arrest: Utah DT suspended indefinitely amid rape accusation - CBS Sports
description: A probable cause affidavit reveals accusations of distributing intimate videos on Snapchat, though formal charges
body:
A probable cause affidavit reveals accusations of distributing intimate videos on Snapchat, though formal charges have not been filed following Wallace's release on bond
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:13 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Utah has suspended defensive tackle Jamal Wallace following an Oct. 11 arrest on suspicion of distributing intimate images via Snapchat. A probable cause affidavit obtained by The Salt Lake Tribune revealed that the woman also accused Wallace of rape.According to the document, the woman claims she met Wallace on Oct. 9 to discuss their relationship, which she described as "off-and-on" dating partners. She alleged that Wallace forced her to engage in various sexual acts, and she later realized that he had taken her phone to record videos.The woman alleges that Wallace sent video of the alleged rape to five people whom she'd been interacting with on Snapchat. After looking through the woman's phone, one officer discovered that Wallace recorded "two sexually explicit videos involving himself and the victim."As part of the investigation, the woman underwent a sexual assault examination.
Wallace has not been formally charged, and he was released on a $5,000 bond. A Utah spokesperson told The Salt Lake Tribune that it is aware of the allegations against Wallace, and he has been suspended indefinitely."We were made aware of the situation with Jamal Wallace on Oct. 11, and he was immediately placed on an indefinite suspension from the program," Utah said in its statement to the Tribune. "We take these matters seriously. As this is a pending legal matter, we have no further comment at this time."
In 2024, Wallace enrolled at Tennessee following a stint in junior college at Sierra College. Following the 2025 campaign, Wallace transferred to Utah and has played in just one game this season.

title: What is illegal forward handing? Bears flagged for one of NFL's rarest penalties - CBS Sports
description: The failed trick play against the Patriots sent viewers sc
body:
The failed trick play against the Patriots sent viewers scrambling to learn about one of the most obscure rules in the NFL rulebook
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:16 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
            
        
                
                
                
            
        
            
                    
                Imagn Images
            
            

    
        There have been thousands of penalties called in the NFL over the past 15 years, but until Thursday night, there was one penalty that had NEVER been called in that span: Illegal forward handing. During the first half of the Bears' game against the Patriots, Chicago got flagged for that exact penalty. If you don't know what "illegal forward handing: is, don't worry, most people don't, and that's because it almost never gets called. 
On the play, Caleb Williams took the snap and immediately handed the ball off to guard Joe Thuney. This was a trick play by the Bears and not only did it NOT work, but they lost five yards after the officiating crew threw a flag. 
The reason you don't see offensive linemen get more handoffs is because in most instances, it's against the rules. As the NFL rule book clearly states, "except where permitted by rule, handing the ball forward to a teammate is illegal."
So what exactly does that mean? It is legal to make a forward handoff behind the line of scrimmage, but only to a player who's eligible to have the ball, such as a running back or a receiver. Giving the ball to an offensive lineman is legal, but only if it's a normal backward handoff.  Once the ball passes the line of scrimmage, you can't have a forward handoff under any circumstances to any player. You also aren't allowed to have a forward handoff after a change of possession. So if a player intercepts a pass, he can't turn around and make a forward handoff to a teammate.Although you can't have a forward handoff in those last two situations, you can have a backward handoff or pitch it backwards to a teammate once your past the line of scrimmage or after a turnover. The penalty on Thursday night marked the first time in 16 years that an illegal forward handoff has been called in a game. According to NFLpenalties.com, the last time this flag was thrown came in a Packers-Lions game on Oct. 3, 2010. In that game, Lions cornerback Chris Houston picked off Aaron Rodgers and then got flagged after he attempted to hand the ball to a teammate who was in front of him. 
This is one of the rarest penalties in the NFL and we all got to witness it on Thursday night.

title: Arizona coach Tommy Lloyd believes NCAA is embracing the eligibility chaos - CBS Sports
description: KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- When I sat down with Tommy Lloyd this week here inside the T-Mobile Center during what amounted to the second half o
body:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- When I sat down with Tommy Lloyd this week here inside the T-Mobile Center during what amounted to the second half of Big 12 Media Days, I expected to talk to the Arizona coach about everything from his rejection of North Carolina to the additions of Caleb Holt and Cameron Holmes.I figured Ivan Kharchenkov might come up. Perhaps even Bryce James.But Diego Pavia?The former Vanderbilt quarterback/future UFL player was nowhere in my notes. But Lloyd is coming off of a Final Four, in charge of one of college basketball's biggest brands, and an obviously smart guy. So before I was done with our conversation about his program and team,  I wanted to get his thoughts about A) Kansas recently, and controversially, enrolling a 24-year-old who was the 59th pick in June's NBA Draft (Trey Kaufman-Renn), B) the NCAA relentlessly challenging five-year-eligibility-period cases connected to 2022 high school graduates, and C) everything else taking up so much oxygen in the sport of college basketball these days.So I did.Then the conversation got really good."My stance on the 5-for-5 is very clear," Lloyd began. "If you're a true 5-for-5 [case], and if the same situation were next year, and you could be eligible without a waiver, you shouldn't be ineligible now. [But] if you're in your sixth or seventh year [of college], and if you've got a story and a bunch of extenuating circumstances, yeah, I'm not too sympathetic to that. So I think what's frustrating for me is [that] when you kind of take a step back and you think about all of the conversations that go on behind the scenes, and, you know, we could go through a few of them here ..."Lloyd trailed off there for a moment."The Pavia Case" is where he picked up before explaining the different ways in which the NCAA is handling things now compared to how it handled them just two years ago when Pavia sued the governing body while arguing that its rules counting his junior college seasons against his Division I eligibility violated the Sherman Antitrust Act by improperly limiting his career and ability to earn name, image, and likeness income potentially worth millions of dollars.
Pavia won his case.His college football career continued thanks to an injunction. Not long after it was granted, the NCAA Division I Board of Directors approved a blanket waiver granting an extra year of eligibility for the 2025-26 academic year to former JUCO and non-NCAA school transfers who were in a position similar to Pavia's."[After the Pavia case], the NCAA ... released a memo to the schools that [more or less said], 'based on this single ruling, we see it can create an uneven playing field among our competitive schools, so we are going to issue a blanket waiver for any kid that's basically in the same circumstances that Pavia was in.' And they did a blanket waiver."Lloyd's point?Why isn't the NCAA issuing a blanket waiver now, considering there are men set to play college basketball in less than two weeks only because they received injunctions from local judges just like Pavia once did? Why isn't the NCAA issuing a blanket waiver now while acknowledging that not doing so would create an unequal playing field based on which players get injunctions and which don't, given that the NCAA did exactly that two years ago after acknowledging that not doing so would, yes, create an unequal playing field based on which players get injunctions and which don't?
Those seem like totally reasonable questions. I asked Lloyd if he had an answer to them/theory about them.Lloyd's theory: Chaos may be the point"I think I do," he answered. "I think my theory is this thing has gotten so political -- and, obviously, there are a lot of things that need to be fixed in college sports," Lloyd said. "So [in my opinion,] the NCAA doesn't mind the 'chaos' right now because it can help drive the case for them to promote the [Protect] College Sports Act, which I'm sure we need."(Translation: The NCAA desperately wants the PCSA to pass ASAP, and it's easier to make the case to the public that college sports needs saving when there are stories weekly about players being ruled eligible and ineligible by local judges for reasons that are inconsistent, confusing and often biased. More specifically, the NCAA's constant legal battles enhance the perception of "chaos" in college sports, which in turn makes it easier for senators like Ted Cruz to insist college sports needs "saving" via a federal law that, as currently constructed, would limit what athletes can make in a way that would otherwise likely be deemed illegal.)
Lloyd's explanation makes as much sense as, if not more sense than, anything anybody else has floated because, he's absolutely right, the NCAA is "digging its heels" in now in one case after another in ways that run completely counter to how it handled similar situations after Pavia's case two years ago.Why?Lloyd thinks the answer is italicized above. If you care, I agree.Either way, Lloyd's larger point, and one I also co-sign, is that just because something might be a smart legal strategy, or a brilliant long-term play, that doesn't make it good or right. As the sixth-year Arizona coach noted, there are lots of men -- exactly 22 just in the Big 12 alone, by his count -- who would be eligible for a fifth year of eligibility if the NCAA's new five-year-eligibility-period rule would've been adopted earlier or if they'd just been born a little later. There's no real difference between them and many of the people we'll all watch play five years of college basketball moving forward or even this season. They were just born roughly a year earlier and enrolled in college when they did."Why should these individual kids [be punished and suffer] real damages?" Lloyd asked. "I mean, there have been guys that have come back for their fifth year and gotten drafted the next year because of that extra year of experience. And there [are players who are] going to make a lot of money [if they are eligible for a fifth year this season]. I mean, there's real damage [being suffered if they can't play this fifth year this season]. So, for me, somebody has to sit down and tell me why this makes sense and how it's good for the sport."
Players caught in the middleLloyd does have a so-called dog in this fight -- namely RJ Godfrey, who graduated high school in 2022, played three years at Clemson, one year at Georgia, graduated, and would now like to play a fifth year at Arizona. A judge in his home state of Georgia initially granted an injunction clearing Godfrey to play. But, more recently, the Georgia Court of Appeals granted the NCAA a stay, leaving Godfrey's future very much up in the air even though older players with less compelling eligibility cases are seemingly good to go thanks to how their legal cases have unfolded in different states with different judges."I get it's complicated -- but you can't tell me it's right that a true 5-for-5 [candidate] that's younger than some of these European players [is ineligible]," Lloyd continued. "[The only difference is] these European players, you know what they didn't do? They didn't redshirt. They [instead] played four years of high-level basketball [professionally] -- and just because they didn't enroll in a school, now they're getting [what amounts to] a [fifth] year of eligibility when our guy, or someone else's guy, enrolled, graduated in four years, and now they're getting penalized for a fifth year because they enrolled right when they graduated out of high school?"It's just tough."I'll take it a step further.Not only would it obviously be unfair and inconsistent if, just to name one case, Trey Kaufman-Renn is allowed to spend a sixth year in a college basketball program and play a fifth this season while Godfrey and other younger players like him aren't allowed to spend a fifth literally in the same conference, all because of rulings by different judges in different places, I'd argue it's also counter-productive to what so many like to call the good of the game.
As I've noted many times on the Eye On College Basketball Podcast, do you realize the number of minutes Matt Norlander and I have spent talking about judges and injunctions this offseason instead of Florida attempting to win a second national title in three years or Jon Scheyer trying to get his first at Duke? Every second spent discussing court rulings is a second not spent on Vanderbilt's Tyler Tanner.It's damaging to the sport.I should've been talking to Tommy Lloyd about Motiejus Krivas. Instead, I talked to him about Diego Pavia.Why?Because the very sensible position the NCAA took two years ago after Pavia's ruling has been abandoned in a way that Lloyd and other coaches find inconsistent and frustrating -- and tied to ulterior motives. While the NCAA is spending millions of dollars fighting against players like Godfrey, most coaches would've preferred it grant a blanket waiver to every 2022 high school graduate, allow them to play a fifth year this season if they wanted to, and if anybody wanted them to, and just be done with it. Doing so would've saved a lot of legal fees and decreased the amount of so-called "chaos" dramatically. It's what coaches wanted -- evidence being Norlander and I asked roughly 100 of them earlier this year, and most of them told us, yes, they would've preferred the 2022 high school graduates be grandfathered in, if only to cut down on the confusion and level the playing field.
But rather than listen to the coaches, or even to the arguments the NCAA itself made just two years earlier about an uneven playing field after Pavia's ruling, the NCAA is out there fighting one legal battle after another, literally from coast to coast, at a cost that can't possibly be sensibly rationalized, all while creating the chaos it swears it wants to end.It makes no sense -- unless the NCAA actually wants the chaos.That's Lloyd's best explanation for what's going on -- going on still, with the season now just 10 days away -- that the NCAA has dug its heels in to fight, fight, fight this time around, in ways that are almost certainly going to create an uneven playing field this college basketball season, and in ways that totally contradict what the same governing body priortized just two years ago, not because its leaders or lawyers believe it's the right or logically consistent thing to do, but rather because it enhances the perception of "chaos" at a time when that perception, real or otherwise, might really be the thing that pushes a controversial bill through the senate and house and turns it into federal law."There's literally going to be an uneven playing field created [this season]" Lloyd said. "And the NCAA is letting it happen."

title: Steelers cancel Paris fan event amid protests; Saints game still on - CBS Sports
description: Sunday's historic game at Stade de France will proceed as planned, with the NFL working alongside local authoriti
body:
Sunday's historic game at Stade de France will proceed as planned, with the NFL working alongside local authorities and increasing security
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:50 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        When the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints meet on Sunday in the NFL's first regular-season game hosted in Paris, they will do so with an intense civil unrest as the backdrop. Protests in the French capital will not impact the NFL Week 7 game, but they did lead to the cancellation of a fan event. The Steelers announced on Thursday that they will not hold the scheduled Steelers House gathering due to the protests.The event was scheduled to unfold over the weekend near the Bastille. There is an authorized march scheduled to begin at Place de la Bastille on Saturday.Sunday's game, meanwhile, will unfold at Stade de France in Saint-Denis, which is located just under six miles from the center of Paris and away from the scheduled demonstrations."Following recent events in the Bastille neighborhood, and after careful consideration, we felt it appropriate not to move forward with the planned Steelers House fan event in Paris," the Steelers said in a statement. "Preparations for Sunday's NFL Paris game at State de France continue as planned, with the NFL working closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters."
There have thus far been no disruptions at NFL sites in the lead-up to Sunday's contest. While concerns over fan and player safety heightened over the last two weeks, the league insisted repeatedly that the game would go on as planned. The NFL first addressed the concerns on Oct. 14 when it stated it looks forward to welcoming fans to Paris later this month.One measure the NFL will enact, though, is an increase in security. NFL executive vice president of club business, international and league events, Peter O'Reilly, said this week that the security presence "will be heightened" as the league works in tandem with local authorities and the U.S. State Department. He said the NFL has had people in Paris since early October and that they are "being very vigilant in everything we do, in all of our planning on an hour-by-hour basis."Former NFL Security Committee member and current CBS Sports analyst Amy Trask said that while teams handle international travel differently from one another, they share similar rules with regard to curfews and activities outside of game day. Trask also detailed the role security plays in these overseas competitions.
"You've got security on site the moment people are approaching the venue," Trask said. "In other words, the security is not simply at the gate when people are entering the venue. There is security well outside of the venue. There is security before you even enter the parking lot, so there will be security throughout the area. Some of the security will be noticeable, recognizable. Some of the security will be undercover, meaning simply not in uniform, not dressed in a manner where you will immediately notice it is security. It was my experience that there is ample security at the NFL events. "... As I noted, when the games are in the United States, that's local security, municipal security, state security, national security. Now you will add to this Parisian security, French security as well."The protests have been ongoing for nearly a month and stem from discontent over the French school system and the nation's cost of living. Protesters, many of them students, called upon the government to address under-resourced schools, poor conditions and teacher shortages. They report, in some cases, that the schools are physically falling apart with crumbling ceilings, water in the walls and rats in the buildings.
Some protests have turned violent. Police arrested thousands of people in connection to the demonstrations and utilized tear gas, stun grenades and other crowd-control measures to address those protests that devolved from peaceful gatherings into riots, according to CBS News.

title: Fantasy football Week 7 injury report: Baker Mayfield nearing return, Emeka Egbuka's status raises concerns - CBS Sports
description: Baker Mayfield is on track to return in Week 7, but Emeka Egbuka's concussion concerns could shake up Tampa's Fan
body:
Baker Mayfield is on track to return in Week 7, but Emeka Egbuka's concussion concerns could shake up Tampa's Fantasy outlook
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:57 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Week 7 is the week when we are potentially getting a lot of injured players back. The Vikings, in particular, look to be getting healthy off their bye. There is optimism that Jordan Addison, T.J. Hockenson, and Jordan Mason will all be returning in Week 7. We're viewing Hockenson as a borderline TE1, Addison as a boom/bust WR3, and Mason as a touchdown-dependent flex. Their return is good news for Kyler Murray, who will have his full complement of weapons in a plus matchup. The additional competition for targets doesn't hamper a No. 1 wide receiver like Justin Jefferson, but it could be a big problem for Aaron Jones.Jones has been a true workhorse running back over the past few weeks, handling three-quarters of the team's rush attempts and a 20% target share. Mason will crush his rush share, and 50% is probably the best-case scenario. Meanwhile, the return of Addison and Hockenson could completely diminish Jones' target share. When all three have been healthy, the running backs have been completely uninvolved in the passing game. I'm still viewing Jones as a low-end RB2, but that is only because the Vikings have an excellent matchup and there could be some rust to shake off for the returners. The sell high window is probably closed.Baker Mayfield back, Emeka Egbuka in concussion protocolThe good news for Tampa Bay is that Baker Mayfield looks like he will return in Week 7. The bad news is Egbuka probably won't. The latter is in the concussion protocol and was listed as a DNP on both Wednesday and Thursday. Mayfield without Egbuka is no more than an upside QB2 with or without Egbuka. If Egbuka is out, we would view Chris Godwin as a WR3, Ted Hurst as an upside flex, and Cade Otton as a decent streaming option. The biggest winner may be Bucky Irving. He has a great matchup and a much higher target share when Mayfield plays. Start him as a borderline RB1.Lamar Jackson practicing on ThursdayJackson technically practiced on Wednesday, though he wasn't there for the media portion and was seen limping afterward. On Thursday he looked better and there is growing optimism he could return. if Jackson is active, you should start him against the Bengals. Zay Flowers is a WR1 with Jackson and a WR2 with Tyler Huntley. Ja'Kobi Lane is a much more appealing flex if Jackson is able to play, especially if Rashod Bateman is not. Mark Andrews has been pretty bad this year, and we don't want to start him, no matter who the quarterback is. 
Zach Charbonnet activatedCharbonnet is slated to return against the Chiefs in Week 7, but we are hesitant to start any Seahawks running back. The Chiefs have one of the best run defenses in the league and this game has a lower over/under. We would expect a healthy split in Charbonnet's return, which makes him a touchdown-dependent flex. We would like to hold Emanuel Wilson for one week, just to be sure of the roles in the backfield, but we certainly don't want to start him.Saquon Barkley back at practiceThere has been optimism that Barkley will play in Week 7, so we are ranking him. He's slightly higher in the rankings than Dameon Pierce was, closer to RB15 than RB20. Hamstrings do have a high recurrence of injury, so if you can hold Pierce, that probably makes sense. It will be interesting to see if Barkley's return causes the Eagles to scrap their extremely high pass rate in Week 6. We're still starting Devonta Smith and Dallas Goedert, but we're nervous.Breece Hall and Adonai Mitchell limitedHall logged a limited session on Thursday, which could have a big impact on the start of the week, Braelon Allen. For now, we're still projecting Hall as out, but he is potentially in play, so be careful if Rhamondre Stevenson and Braelon Allen are your only two options. If Hall returns, we expect him to lead the backfield and be an RB2, while Allen has a bigger role than he did earlier in the year and is a touchdown-dependent flex. Mitchell could dampen out excitement for Omar Cooper as well. We wouldn't want to start any Jets receiver besides Garrett Wilson if Mitchell returns.
David Montgomery out againWoody Marks will lead the backfield, and his rush share could be even higher with Jawhar Jordan placed on IR. This is a very good matchup against the Giants that should provide both a fantastic game script and improved rushing efficiency. Marks is best viewed as an RB2, though he could have RB1 usage and if he scores a touchdown, he could produce top-12 results. Start him.Jeremiyah Love still not readyThis will once again be a split between Tyler Allgeier and Zonovan "Bam" Knight. Knight had the hot hand in Week 6, but we still expect Allgeier to get the first crack at the Broncos suspect run defense. If Knight breaks another long run, then he could absolutely be the best Cardinals back but this is a low-confidence situation. It's best to view both of these backs as low-end flexes; we prefer Allgeier, but not by much.Dalton Schultz limited on ThursdaySchultz didn't practice Wednesday and was limited onThursday, so you should probably be wary about starting him in Week 7. At the very least, you should start Hunter Henry and Colston Loveland over Schultz and prepare a backup plan. If Schultz is out, we aren't going to start another Texans tight end but we may be more interested in flexing Marvin Harrison Jr. or Jaylin Noel.
Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson limited on ThursdayHead Coach Todd Monken has expressed optimism about both players returning in Week 7, so we are ranking them. Judkins is a low-end RB2 in what should be a good game script, while Sampson is best viewed as a PPR flex. The Browns have thrown to their running backs much more than we expected and we will be interested to see how those targets are distributed if their top two backs are healthy.

title: Eagles Saquon Barkley trade proposals: Giants, Bengals among six destinations - CBS Sports
description: A return to New York headlines six potential landing spots for Barkley if Philadelphia decides to reset its roste
body:
A return to New York headlines six potential landing spots for Barkley if Philadelphia decides to reset its roster
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:26 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Philadelphia Eagles might be at an inflection point in their championship contention window. Injuries to myriad starters, the loss of Jalen Hurts for the season, Lane Johnson's retirement and an offense that cannot seem to get off the ground raise questions about whether general manager Howie Roseman tears his roster down at the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline. If he does, star running back Saquon Barkley might be headed out of town.Trading Barkley would be the ultimate admission that the Eagles, as currently constructed, cannot achieve their goals. The financial impact of moving him will lock this franchise into a rebuild, as he carries a salary cap hit of $26.4 million in dead money for 2027. At the same time, the large sum of unusable cap space gives the Eagles leverage over trade partners in that they can drive up the price. Suitors could also be inclined to pay up, considering Barkley is only guaranteed $2.5 million next season and has no guaranteed money in the final year of his contract in 2028.On the other hand, Barkley is an aging running back who will turn 30 years old the week before the Super Bowl. He has not been able to replicate the magic of his career-best 2024 season, so the former NFL Offensive Player of the Year's best days may be behind him. That could make teams tepid about spending first-round draft capital in a potential trade.There are a number of teams that need help at running back, and despite the questions about Barkley's longevity, he would likely elevate their offenses to a significant degree.
Here are six potential trades that would move Barkley out of Philadelphia.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    New York GiantsGiants receive: Saquon BarkleyEagles receive: Cam Skattebo, 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pickIn such a weak NFC East, the division-leading Giants have a path to the playoffs, but they need a functional run game to get there. Even with their abundance of options, it seems John Harbaugh does not know who to deploy at running back (especially if you ask Najee Harris). Reuniting with Barkley eliminates all questions. Plus, Harbaugh himself said this week that it would be "great" to be in a "Saquon Barkley circumstance" where the Giants had a clear-cut No. 1 ballcarrier.A return to New York makes plenty of sense for Barkley, but it would likely cost the Giants a premium to pull it off, given the intra-division nature of the trade. For multiple years of control of the Eagles' star running back, they may have to part with their own top running back asset in addition to meaningful draft capital.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Seattle SeahawksSeahawks receive: Saquon BarkleyEagles receive: Emanuel Wilson, 2027 third-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pickDeclining to bring Kenneth Walker III back in free agency has haunted the Seahawks, especially with Zach Charbonnet missing the first six games due to the torn ACL he sustained last season. The offense is far more ineffective than it was during last year's Super Bowl run because of the nonexistence of the run game, which ranks second-worst in EPA per rush. Charbonnet will return in Week 7, but he is not a bellcow back, and first-round rookie Jadarian Price is still on injured reserve. Seattle should make a run at a lead running back to revitalize an offense that, in its current form, is not good enough to make another deep postseason push.
Barkley's arrival would create a logjam at the position, so Seattle may try to send one back to Philadelphia. And with three third-rounders and three fifth-rounders in its coffers, those are the picks that make the most sense to move.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Minnesota VikingsVikings receive: Saquon Barkley, 2027 seventh-round pickEagles receive: 2027 third-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pickThe recent trade history between the Vikings and Eagles makes them sensible partners for another deal. Minnesota holds Philadelphia's upcoming third-round pick, while Philadelphia owns Minnesota's seventh-rounder in next year's draft thanks to the Jonathan Greenard trade they completed in April. Those picks could go back to their original homes if these teams do business with each other once again.
The Vikings' run game is serviceable and is in line for a boost with Jordan Mason set to come off injured reserve this week. But the pairing of Mason and Aaron Jones is only that: Serviceable. Barkley would be a clear upgrade for an offense that ranks in the bottom half of the league in scoring and yards per game. Bolstering that group should be a priority as Minnesota attempts to capitalize on its league-best defense and keep its perfect start to the season rolling.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Cincinnati BengalsBengals receive: Saquon BarkleyEagles receive: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pickThe name value alone of an offense that boasts Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Saquon Barkley would be tremendous. Imagine what it would deliver in terms of production. The Bengals' typically unstoppable unit is limited in 2026 by a run game that ranks just 27th in yards per game, so a boost on the ground would open all kinds of opportunities for Burrow downfield and rekindle that elite attack. Chase Brown has been a disappointment to the point where Samaje Perine is becoming an increasingly large part of the ground game. That signals a cry for help at the running back position.As the Bengals attempt to cash in during Burrow's prime, this is the time to mortgage the future and invest draft picks in splashy trades like one for Barkley.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Denver BroncosBroncos receive: Saquon BarkleyEagles receive: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pickSean Payton already reclaimed play-calling duties, but that might not be enough to save the Broncos' offense. Something else is clearly missing from this unit. Long-term assets like RJ Harvey and Jonah Coleman make the future of the running back group bright, but it is underperforming right now, and that is a problem for a team that has Super Bowl aspirations. An infusion of immediate help would lower J.K. Dobbins and Harvey a rung each on the depth chart, and perhaps that is precisely what the group needs while Coleman recovers on injured reserve.The Broncos are flush with 2027 late-round picks, so moving a Day 3 selection in addition to a second-rounder would not hurt.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Houston TexansTexans receive: Saquon BarkleyEagles receive: Woody Marks, 2027 seventh-round pick, 2028 second-round pickThe David Montgomery trade is aging like a bust of a move as he cedes work to Woody Marks in a disappointing run game. It would be an admission that the move did not pan out as expected if general manager Nick Caserio traded for another running back, but it might be a worthwhile one if it takes an otherwise surprisingly effective offense to another level. C.J. Stroud is playing the best football of his career and looks determined to pull the Texans out of the 0-4 hole they dug themselves into but might have trouble doing so if the ground game is a drag.
That the Texans hold the Eagles' 2027 seventh-round pick (which has already changed hands thrice) could aid in their pursuit of Barkley, even if it is just a throw-in as the final sweetener in the trade package.

Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.
Where to watch Bears vs. Patriots liveDate: Thursday, Oct. 22 | Time: 8:20 p.m. ETLocation: Soldier Field (Chicago)Streaming: Amazon PrimeFollow: CBS Sports AppOdds: Bears -3, O/U 50.5 via DraftKings SportsbookWhen the Patriots have the ballDrake Maye has found himself over the last three weeks, completing 66 of 103 passes for 878 yards, 10 touchdowns, and one interception after going just 51-of-80 for 585 yards, one touchdown, and six picks through the first three games of the season. Maye has rediscovered the deep ball, in particular, going 12 of 20 for 350 yards and four scores on throws beyond 15 yards in the last three games, per Tru Media. Before that, he was just 9 of 20 for 281 yards and four interceptions on those throws.Maye finished with a strong game against the Jets despite A.J. Brown looking horrifyingly bad in his return from an ankle injury. Brown dropped (at least) three passes and turned his 10 targets into only 27 yards. Maye also lost Romeo Doubs to a shoulder injury on an early-game touchdown pass, so he was working with a limited receiving corps behind Brown. Still, he threw for 235 yards and three touchdowns without turning the ball over. Brown will presumably be better here, and Chicago hasn't been great against outside receivers, but last week's return of Kyler Gordon could lead to slot man Demario Douglas having a tougher go of things than he has over the last few weeks. Kyle Williams could get in on the action with Doubs sidelined, though Efton Chism has been getting more snaps because the Patriots trust him as a blocker.
Chicago checks in a surprising eighth in opponents' EPA per dropback so far this season, per Tru Media, thanks to a high sack rate and a few timely interceptions. Opponents have averaged 8.4 yards per attempt against the Bears, though, indicating that you can indeed move the ball through the air if you can get a pass off and avoid a turnover. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has generated pressure at an above-average rate (39.7% of dropbacks) despite working with a somewhat limited group up front, and the Patriots will be without two starting guards here. So, the running backs (particularly Rhamondre Stevenson) will have to be on their game in pass protection on Thursday night.The Patriots have struggled to run the ball thus far this season, with Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson and Corey Kiner combining for an average of just 3.9 yards per carry on 151 rushing attempts. Stevenson leads the way in the backfield largely because the Patriots trust him the most in short yardage and pass protection, but he hasn't been efficient or explosive. Henderson had an explosive rushing touchdown on his first run of the season but has failed to record one since. 
Kiner was a little-used third-stringer until he salted away the game against the Jets last Sunday. He could perhaps work his way into more touches after a nice showing in that game, given the rushing struggles of the two leads and the fact that Henderson also fumbled against New York.The Bears have allowed opponents 4.4 yards per carry on running-back rushes so far this season, with much of the success coming by way of yards before contact. It may be difficult for the Patriots to generate those types of yards with their injury issues along the offensive line, and their backs haven't exactly done the best job of breaking tackles this year, so the challenge of moving the offense down the field will likely fall squarely on Maye's right shoulder.When the Bears have the ballCaleb Williams returned last week from a three-game absence due to a hamstring injury and looked no worse for wear. Williams completed 30 of 36 passes for 305 yards and a touchdown. The Bears kept things simple for him with a 3.9-yard average depth of throw (eighth-lowest for any quarterback in a single game this season), per Tru Media, and he was extremely efficient as a result. 
Williams has only played in three games so far this year, but he's leading the league with a 72.5% completion rate and is up to a career-best 7.8 yards per attempt. And that's despite a truly awful game against the Vikings in Week 2, where he went 15-of-26 for just 138 yards and an interception. In his first couple of appearances, it seemed like journeyman wideout Kalif Raymond (14 targets in Weeks 1 and 2) was his primary option, but on Sunday, it was Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland -- the most expected options -- leading the way with eight and seven targets, respectively. Rome Odunze saw five looks. Given the way they're each deployed, it seems likely that Odunze will see a bunch of Christian Gonzalez's coverage on Thursday night -- especially with Carlton Davis III ruled out. Odunze is the biggest of the trio and plays most often on the perimeter, and he also tends to run the most routes. If that's the way things go, we should expect the passing game to flow through Burden and Loveland yet again. The Patriots have allowed opponents to complete 31 of 46 passes for 301 yards on throws to the slot this season, per Tru Media. Burden could have a nice night working inside if he's on the field more often than he was last week (eight targets on only 18 routes), though Marcus Jones does have an interception this season and is allowing only 1.46 yards per coverage snap in the slot, per Pro Football Focus. 
By contrast, New England has allowed only 29 catches for 279 yards to tight ends to date, so Loveland may not find the coverage as friendly. The Bears would do well to line him up all over the formation rather than solely in line, and perhaps use multi-tight end sets where he plays more of a receiver role, and Cole Kmet or Sam Roush handles the blocking aspects of the position.The Bears also tried against Atlanta to do what they do best: run the ball with volume. D'Andre Swift and Roschon Johnson (the latter filling in for the injured Kyle Monangai) combined for 29 carries. They ran for only 96 yards on those totes, but they did find the end zone three times. Chicago's offensive line actually created some nice push, generating 1.45 yards before contact per carry, according to Tru Media, but the backs slumped to only 1.83 yards after contact, as they combined for only four broken tackles. (For context, consider that the Seahawks' running backs combined for 10 in their awful game against the Broncos on Thursday night.)
The Pats have allowed only 3.9 yards per rush this season, thanks in part to yielding an average of only 0.75 yards before contact. Swift and Johnson (Monangai is out again) will have to do a better job of breaking tackles this time around if they want to generate yardage and create favorable down-and-distance scenarios for Williams and the passing game.PredictionI see this being a high-scoring game, what with two offenses that can pile up points quickly. Chicago's offense in two non-rain/non-Brian Flores games with Caleb Williams under center has been electric, particularly on the ground, and Caleb Williams opens things up for the passing game. New England is struggling to run the ball, but Drake Maye has been on fire as of late. I'll lean toward the Bears here because of the Patriots' injury issues along the offensive line, which could hold the run game back further and put even more on Maye's shoulders. Prediction: Bears 31, Patriots 27

With Dallas sitting at 2-4, Schottenheimer acknowledged that he must coach better

        Brian Schottenheimer and his offense are feeling the heat after a 2-4 start.The Cowboys have scored fewer than 20 points in consecutive Dak Prescott starts for the first time in seven seasons, and Dallas has work to do to compete for the NFC East crown.One of the players now carrying the blame for Dallas' 31st-ranked rushing offense is George Pickens. Pickens' 1,429 receiving yards in 2025 ranked third in the NFL, and his 428 this season sit outside of the top 10. However, Schottenheimer has issued a different type of challenge to his Pro Bowl receiver."I think GP is one of those guys where I don't ever see him really affected in terms of the emotion of does he get the ball? Does he not get the ball? These guys play a lot of snaps. ... He needs to understand that he impacts us in the running game as well," Schottenheimer said. "He needs to understand that he impacts us in the running game as well. He's got to do the same thing in the run game, picking up safeties and blocking corners, just like Javonte [Williams] does, picking up blitzes so he can catch balls. That's part of the team-first mindset, and GP does understand that. When he's going, they're going to play soft inside. When he's not going, the safeties get pretty good runs at our backs. And that's got to improve."  
Schottenheimer takes accountability for play callingDallas' offense has become too simplistic in Year 2 under Schottenheimer in 2026. This season, the Cowboys rank as second-to-last in the NFL in motion rate (42.7%), 28th out of 32 teams in under-center rate (30.4%) and 20th in play action rate. "I think some of it is deserved," Schottenheimer said of the criticism coming his way. "We got to play better. I got to coach better. And so when you grow up in a family that your dad's a head coach for over 20-something years [21 years], you understand that this is part of the job description. No one likes it. I block out most of it. Some of it gets to me doing this job and having to speak to you guys is part of that. But at the same time, I've got strong shoulders. I know what a great coach I am. I know what this team is capable of, and that's what I focus on."Cowboys offensive tendencies under Brian Schottenheimer, Since 2025 (NFL ranks)20252026Motion rate56.6% (13th)42.7% (31st)Play action rate28.2% (9th)24.2% (20th)Under center rate38.4% (11th)30.4% (28th)Shotgun rate61.6% (22nd)69.6% (5th)Run rate41.5% (24th)32.5% (Last)Tempo (average time between snaps in seconds)32.9 (Fastest)33.4 (Fastest)So how does Schottenheimer plan to fix the run game? By calling more runs to allow Williams to get in more of a rhythm. However, the caveat he threw out is that Dallas should not fall behind early in games. The Cowboys have spent the fifth-most time trailing (3:23:30) in the NFL this season. 
"I think it starts with calling more runs, which requires being in more, I keep using the word normal, close games where you're not having a play from behind," Schottenheimer said. "I do think that the more you run it, the better you feel. You figure out combination blocks and things like that. I will say early on in most of our games, we've not run it as well as we are capable of. And there's been times where again, as the head coach and the play caller, I have to make the decision of, 'okay, clock says X, we're down X, what is it? All right, it's time to go.' So those are decisions that we discuss and we make those decisions, but it starts with just letting these guys get into a groove, let these guys get bats at the plate, if you will. And that's a big part."

body:
The Hall of Fame running back said he was diagnosed after noticing an issue with his hand and has been managing the condition through treatment
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:10 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Marshall Faulk, an NFL legend and the coach at Southern University, revealed that he has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, a progressive disorder of the central nervous system affecting the body's movement. Faulk, 53, said that he has been dealing with the disease for about 18 months. He first realized that something was wrong when he was having issues with his hand while playing golf. He mentioned the issue to his doctor during a routine physical. "I was like, 'Wow, is that something?'" Faulk said on an episode of "Caring Neurologist" with Dr. Sandeep Thakkar. "'Is that normal?' And the doctor was— he literally was like, 'You need to go get checked.'"  Faulk is in good spirits and considers himself lucky because he got the diagnosis early. He said that it can be managed through treatment while comparing it to recovering from injuries during his NFL career. Since getting treatment, Faulk said that he has become more active, is sleeping more and that his life is relatively the same. He said that while he still experiences rigidity in his hands, the condition has not gotten worse. 
"The little tremors that I get, you know, they are what they are," he said. "I just pay attention to my gait, you know, while I walk, when I'm working out, my ability to balance. It's still where it is."  Faulk wants to advocate for people to seek help if they experience symptoms. Surprisingly, he said that he had not had a conversation about his diagnosis with his family or friends.  "If it comes a time to where my lifestyle changes, then I will," he said. "Then that conversation could be had. I'm functioning. I'm good. You know, I just I think I caught it early. I'm in a good place."  
Faulk was named Southern's coach on Dec. 1, 2025. He previously served as Deion Sanders' running backs coach at Colorado. A 2011 Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee, Faulk is widely considered one of the greatest running backs of all time. At San Diego State, he led the FBS in rushing three straight years. He finished second in the Heisman Trophy voting in 1992 and was fourth in the voting in 1993. Faulk was the No. 2 overall pick in the 1994 NFL Draft. He earned two Pro Bowls with the Colts before entering another stratosphere after he was traded to the Rams in 1999. That season, Faulk helped the Rams win the Super Bowl while becoming the second player to post 1,000 yards rushing and receiving in the same season. 
Faulk won league MVP in 2000 after he led the NFL in touchdown runs (18) and yards-per-carry average (5.4). He helped the Rams get back to the Super Bowl in 2001. A seven-time Pro Bowler and three-time All-Pro, Faulk retired after the 2005 season with 12,279 rushing yards, 6,875 receiving yards, 100 rushing touchdowns and 136 total touchdowns. He, Marcus Allen and Tiki Barber are the only players in NFL history with 10,000 rushing and 5,000 career receiving yards.

In the words of their teammates, two of the best -- and youngest -- players on the Rays and Brewers are ready for the bright lights

        MILWAUKEE -- World Series discussions often center around the superstars -- especially if there are those easy ones we can call "future Hall of Famers." Two years ago, when the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees faced off, there were at least five active players that fit the bill and probably a few more with a decent chance. This time around, the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays don't have any surefire Hall of Famers. Christian Yelich is the closest thing, and he might be short (it's a different discussion for a different time).  I think there's a good argument to be made, however, that the best position player on each team is, in fact, a future Hall of Famer. It's far too early to make such a declaration, but they have the early foundation and the required talent. Both are emerging superstars, though one is a little more nationally established than the other (thank you, Home Run Derby). They'll get their spotlight together in this series. We're speaking, of course, about Junior Caminero of the Rays and Jackson Chourio of the Brewers. Now, they aren't unknowns. I'm not suggesting that. But I'll also excuse you if you don't regularly watch either of these teams. Regardless, we are all about to be blessed with a significant part of the next wave of incredible baseball talent. 
Caminero is a 23-year-old Dominican third baseman. His first full-time season was 2025, during which he clubbed 45 homers with 110 RBI. As an encore this season, he hit 42 home runs with 101 RBI. Don't mistake the line as regression. Though the power numbers dipped ever so slightly there, he raised his average by 12 points, his on-base percentage by 49 points and his walk rate by five percentage points, all while his strikeout rate dropped. To see this type of growth from one year to the next at age 23 while nearly maintaining his power leads me to believe there's an untapped extra gear in him as a player. We might well see him hit close to .300 next season and duplicate those 40 bombs. He also improved on defense, helping him vault to 5.7 WAR from last season's 4.3."I think the upside is just the consistency," Rays outfielder Cedric Mullins said on Thursday. "He's put some fantastic seasons together in back-to-back years. Even when he started off a little slow, he bounced back with a crazy hot streak. It's going to be exciting to see what he can do moving forward."
"Junior is a special player, special teammate," Rays manager Kevin Cash said earlier in the playoffs. "He's been incredible and would expect that, just as he's done every single stop throughout his career, whether it's playing winter ball or coming up, he's going to be very excited, motivated, and we'll rise to the occasion."
Caminero might well finish in the top two of MVP voting, behind favorite Yordan Alvarez, and I've seen enough to say with decent certainty that he's a future MVP. Rays catcher Liam Hicks, acquired at the trade deadline, raved about something as simple as getting to watch Caminero in batting practice every day, but focused specifically on his ability to adjust and adapt at the big-league level."That's the crazy thing, too: how much power he has, how many home runs he hits," Hicks said. "He doesn't strike out a lot; he makes a ton of contact. I think that part of his game is just crazy. He's got as much upside as anyone in the game."
Chourio, meanwhile, is a 22-year-old Venezuelan (and World Baseball Classic champion!) who signed an eight-year extension before he even debuted in the majors. He started playing professionally at age 17 in the Brewers system and was a top five prospect in all of baseball by 2023, when he was just 19. There's a five-tool superstar in here just waiting to have a monster breakout season. Here in 2026, he had his best year, but there's clearly more in the tank. Remember, he's only 22. Injuries held him to 127 games this year, but he still hit .291/.351/.487 (129 OPS+) with 27 doubles, 25 home runs, 75 RBI, 96 runs, 23 steals and 4.9 WAR. He's a Gold Glove finalist and he's gone 20-20 in all three of his MLB seasons so far. He can do it all. "Chourio is, he's special, man," Brewers pitcher Chad Patrick said on Thursday during media day. "When you watch him in the box, his presence, his tone, he's capable of being anything he wants to be in the box."His day-in, day-out is just happy. He's a happy guy."
"The ceiling he has is so high that we don't know if he'll ever hit it," reliever DL Hall said. "You know, just because he just keeps getting better and better and it seems like there's no limit."
"Playing with him every day for me and the rest of the bullpen, every time he gets up, we're like, 'he's probably gonna hit a homer.' Every single time he comes up to the plate, you just expect something special. It speaks to the work he puts in and how focused he is, especially at such a young age." It's impossible to miss the talent just oozing out of Chourio. There's an earned swagger that says we ain't seen nothin' yet. Another future MVP? He absolutely has the talent, even if he's further away than Caminero at this point -- and that's no insult. Chourio has also shown a flair for the dramatic."No moment's too big for Jack Jack," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after NLCS Game 3, when Chourio hit a first-pitch home run off former Cy Young winner Blake Snell. "He's special."
Brewers pitcher Dustin May has seen his fair share of talented teammates, including the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Cody Bellinger and Christian Yelich. And that's only naming his teammates who have won MVPs. "I can't say no," May said when CBS Sports asked if Chourio would join that list. "He's definitely got it in there, for sure. If he can put it together one year like I know he can, he'll win one.""I think [MVP upside] is there for sure," said Patrick. "He's learned the game over the last three years and he definitely has the upside to win it." 
Caminero and Chourio, the young studs of their respective clubs, are different players. The former is a corner infielder and prototypical middle-order slugger, even if he's more well-rounded than some might believe that term implies. The latter is an outfielder with great speed, capable of a 30-30 season as soon as next year, but he's unlikely to get up into the mid-40s in home runs the way Caminero figures to do annually. Caminero won't steal a ton of bases, while Chourio could well go for 40+ someday. But no matter the skill set, they have something undeniably in common: they're the best position players on their team at a tender, young age. The 2026 World Series is a showcase for these two uber-talented players. It probably won't be the last.
